title: Scenario: Ransomware Alert
context: It is 02:14. The SIEM reports a series of encrypted file creations on server FIN-01, followed by a ransom note. You are the on-call analyst.

n1.text: Which indicator most directly confirms ransomware?

choices.text: An increase in outbound DNS traffic
choices.why: It is a possible signal, but non-specific.

choices.text: Hundreds of files renamed with the same extension and a ransom note
choices.why: Mass extension renaming and a ransom note are the behavioral signature of ransomware.

choices.text: A failed login on an account

n2.text: You find an outbound connection to an unknown IP. Which IOC do you record as a priority?

choices.text: The IP address, timestamp, and process hash
choices.why: IP, timestamp, and hash are actionable IOCs for correlation and blocking.
Too sparse: impossible to correlate or block.

choices.text: The color of the alert in the SIEM
choices.why: The color is a display attribute, not investigation data.

n3.text: The responsible process is `powershell.exe` with an encoded string. What is the most likely interpretation?

choices.why: An encoded string and encryption behavior point toward malicious use.
Abuse of native tools with an encoded payload is typical of fileless malware.
The artifacts are consistent with one another: this is not rule noise.

n4.outcome: You qualified the attack, collected IOCs, and identified the fileless vector: three key reflexes for objective 2.5.

debrief: Ransomware is confirmed by encryption behavior and the ransom note, not an isolated alert.
A useful IOC is precise, timestamped, and shareable (IP, domain, hash, path).
Abuse of PowerShell with an encoded string points to fileless / living-off-the-land.
